content: Citrus canker is a disease that affects citrus species and is caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas axonopodis. This infection results in the formation of lesions on the leaves, stems, and fruit of citrus trees, including lime, oranges, and grapefruit. While the disease does not pose a threat to human health, it significantly impacts the health of citrus trees, leading to premature leaf and fruit drop. Although fruit infected with citrus canker is safe for consumption, its appearance makes it unsuitable for sale. The disease is believed to have originated in Southeast Asia and is highly persistent once established in an area. Successful eradication often requires the destruction of all citrus orchards in the affected region. Currently, outbreaks of citrus canker are ongoing in Australia, Brazil, and the United States. Biology The bacterium Xanthomonas axonopodis is a rod-shaped, gram-negative organism equipped with polar flagella. Its genome is approximately 5 megabase pairs in length. There are several types of citrus canker caused by different pathovars and variants of this bacterium: The Asiatic type (Canker A), caused by X. axonopodis pv. citri, is the most widespread and severe form of the disease. It originated in Asia. Cancrosis B, caused by X. axonopodis pv. aurantifolii, primarily affects lemons, key lime, bitter orange, and pomelo. It originated in South America. Cancrosis C, also caused by X. axonopodis pv. aurantifolii, infects only key lime and bitter orange. A-strains, found in Oman, Saudi Arabia, Iran, and India, exclusively infect key lime. Pathology Plants infected with citrus canker exhibit characteristic lesions on leaves, stems, and fruit. These lesions are raised, brown, and have water-soaked margins, often surrounded by a yellow halo or ring. Older lesions develop a corky texture but may still retain the halo effect. The bacterium propagates within these lesions, which ooze bacterial cells. These cells can be dispersed by wind and rain, spreading the infection to other plants in the vicinity. Large storm events, such as tornadoes and hurricanes, can further facilitate the spread of the disease. Additionally, contaminated equipment, workers who have come into contact with infected trees, and the transport of infected or contaminated plants or fruit can also spread the disease. The bacteria can enter a plant through its stomata or through wounds on leaves or other green parts. Young leaves are particularly susceptible to infection. Damage caused by citrus leaf miner larvae (Phyllocnistis citrella) can also create entry points for the bacteria. Symptoms of the disease typically appear 14 to 60 days or more after infection. The bacteria can remain viable in old lesions and on other plant surfaces for several months. Detection Citrus canker can be identified in orchards and on fruit by the appearance of its characteristic lesions. Early detection is critical, especially in quarantine situations. Pathogenicity testing involves inoculating multiple citrus species with the bacterium. Concurrently, other diagnostic tests, such as antibody detection, fatty-acid profiling, and genetic procedures using PCR, are conducted to identify the specific strain of the bacterium. Susceptibility Most citrus varieties are susceptible to citrus canker, although some species are more vulnerable than others. A few species exhibit resistance to infection. Management Citrus canker outbreaks are managed and prevented through various measures. In countries where the disease is not present, quarantine measures are implemented to prevent its introduction. In regions with new outbreaks, eradication programs initiated soon after detection have been successful. These programs typically involve the destruction of affected orchards. In cases where eradication has failed and the disease has become established, management strategies include replacing susceptible citrus cultivars with resistant ones, applying preventive sprays of copper-based bactericides, and destroying infected trees along with all surrounding trees within an appropriate radius. Distribution and Economic Impact Citrus canker is thought to have originated in Southeast Asia and India. It is now also present in Japan, South and Central Africa, the Middle East, the Pacific Islands, some countries in South America, and Florida. While some regions have successfully eradicated the disease or have ongoing eradication programs, citrus canker remains endemic in most areas where it has appeared. Due to its rapid spread, high potential for damage, and impact on export sales and domestic trade, citrus canker poses a significant threat to all citrus-growing regions. Australia The citrus industry is the largest fresh-fruit exporting industry in Australia. The country has experienced three outbreaks of citrus canker, two of which were successfully eradicated, while one is ongoing. The disease was first detected in the Northern Territory in 1912, leading to the destruction of all citrus trees north of latitude 19° South, a process that took 11 years. In 2004, Asiatic citrus canker was detected in an orchard in Emerald, Queensland, likely due to the illegal importation of infected citrus plants. The state and federal governments ordered the destruction of all commercial orchards, non-commercial citrus trees, and native lime trees (C. glauca) in the vicinity of Emerald to prevent further spread. Brazil Citrus is a vital domestic and export crop for Brazil, with São Paulo being the largest sweet orange production area in the world. The state has over 100,000 orchards, and the area planted with citrus is increasing. However, the uniformity of citrus varieties in São Paulo has made the region particularly vulnerable to citrus canker, resulting in significant crop and monetary losses. In Brazil, eradication efforts involve destroying contaminated trees and those within a 30-meter radius. By 1998, over half a million trees had been destroyed. United States Citrus canker was first identified in the United States in 1910 near the Georgia-Florida border. The disease spread rapidly southward, reaching Dade County, Florida, within two years. Beyond Florida, the pathogen spread throughout the Gulf States and as far north as South Carolina. Efforts to control the disease cost $5 million at the time (equivalent to $28 million in 2000 dollars). In 26 counties, 257,745 grove trees and 3,093,110 nursery trees were destroyed by burning. Citrus canker was detected again in Florida in 1986 and successfully eradicated. However, a new outbreak was discovered in 1995 near Miami International Airport. Despite eradication attempts, the disease had spread across much of the state by late 2005, likely facilitated by hurricanes in 2004 and 2005. Active eradication programs continue in 13 Florida counties, and sentinel tree surveys are conducted statewide to detect new infections. The spread of the disease following Hurricane Wilma in October 2005 has been linked to a significant drop in citrus production estimates. A USDA study indicated that the spread could lead to the destruction of over 183,000 acres (741 km²), representing an additional 25% of the total citrus area.
